jurisdiction: City of New York (all five boroughs)
official_title: Proposal Number 1, a Question. Proposed Charter Amendment: Speed Up Process for Granting a Revocable Consent to Use Public Space. Simplify process to use public space for uses such as ramps, planters and cafes, by removing mandatory hearings and Council disapproval of sidewalk cafes, while maintaining community and Council input. “Yes” speeds up process to use public space while maintaining community input. “No” maintains longer process with mandatory public hearing to use public space and Council review of sidewalk cafes.
plain_summary: Speeds up permits to use sidewalks and streets for things like outdoor cafes, ramps, benches and planters. Public hearings become optional, paid newspaper notices end, and the City Council can no longer vote down a sidewalk cafe. Community boards and local officials still get notice and can comment.
yes_means: Hearings on permits to use sidewalks and streets become optional, newspaper notices end, and the City Council can no longer reject individual sidewalk cafes.
no_means: Each of these permits keeps its required public hearing and newspaper notices, and the City Council can still reject individual sidewalk cafes.
current_law: The Department of Transportation (or, for telecom equipment, the Office of Technology and Innovation) must hold a public hearing on each revocable consent; the applicant must pay to publish notice twice in local newspapers; notice runs in the City Record for 15 days; the Mayor must approve. Sidewalk cafes also get community board review, and the City Council can vote to disapprove them. The City can revoke any consent at any time, and holders pay an annual fee. The Commission says sidewalk cafe applications now take 6 to 8 months and roadway cafes 3 to 5.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal note was found. The Charter Revision Commission estimates savings for small businesses of up to $1,800 per application in requirement costs (newspaper notices alone can run up to $1,500) and says outdoor dining approvals would drop from about eight months to about two.
pass_threshold: Simple majority of NYC voters who vote on the question. Each proposal passes or fails on its own.
confusing_wording_note: 'While maintaining community and Council input' is true only in a narrower sense: community boards and local officials can still comment, but required hearings end and the full Council loses its vote on sidewalk cafes. It also covers more than restaurants, including ramps, benches, planters and telecom equipment. 'Revocable consent' means a permit the City can take back at any time.

supporters_case.text: Citizens Union calls it "a straightforward, positive step to improve the outdoor dining culture," saying cafe approvals have become so slow and costly that fewer licenses are being issued. The Commission says hearings are sparsely attended, newspaper ads can cost up to $1,500, and the Council's call-up power was used only 10 to 15 times a year but adds up to 30 days to every sidewalk cafe application. As of July 6, 2026, the City had fully issued 1,549 outdoor dining licenses, compared with about 11,770 restaurants during the pandemic program.

opponents_case.text: Common Cause New York recommends no: "Government efficiency is important, but it should not come at the expense of public participation and legislative oversight." The City Council said several of the five proposals could reduce public input and weaken checks and balances, though it did not ask voters to reject them.

jurisdiction: City of New York (all five boroughs)
official_title: Proposal Number 2, a Question. Proposed Charter Amendment: Reduce City Contractor Paperwork; Require Regular Meetings of Procurement Policy Board. Reduce paperwork for City contractors by authorizing Procurement Policy Board to simplify contractor questionnaire. Require quarterly meetings of the Procurement Policy Board. Remove mandatory hearing for required client services report. “Yes” amends Procurement Policy Board authority, including to simplify contractor questionnaire; authorizes Mayor to delegate certain contract approvals. “No” leaves laws unchanged, with Mayor and Comptroller maintaining longer questionnaire.
plain_summary: Lets a City board shorten and tailor the long questionnaire every would-be City contractor fills out, and requires that board to meet every three months. It also drops one required hearing and lets the mayor hand approval of some large no-bid contracts to agency officials.
yes_means: A City board can shorten the contractor questionnaire and must meet every three months, and the mayor can let agency officials approve some large contracts.
no_means: Contractors keep the same long questionnaire, the board has no required meeting schedule, and today's approval and hearing rules stay.
current_law: The questionnaire's questions are set in local law and apply to every contractor; the Mayor and Comptroller jointly maintain it. Agencies that award client-services contracts (shelters, job training, youth programs) must publish a draft plan, hold a hearing, then publish a final plan each year. The mayor cannot delegate approval of contracts over $5 million that are not competitively bid. A state law allowing public comment periods instead of hearings on contract awards expires at the end of 2030. The Procurement Policy Board has no required meeting schedule.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal note was found. The Commission says these changes could cut roughly a month from a procurement and save hundreds of hours of agency staff time. In fiscal year 2025 the City spent $42.3 billion, nearly 40% of its budget, on outside contractors.
pass_threshold: Simple majority of NYC voters who vote on the question. Each proposal passes or fails on its own.
confusing_wording_note: Two parts are easy to miss. The summary line doesn't mention that the mayor could hand approval of some no-bid contracts over $5 million to agency officials (only the 'Yes' line hints at it), and neither line mentions making permanent the switch from in-person hearings to written comments on many contract awards. 'Client services report' means each agency's yearly plan for contracts like shelters and youth programs; the hearing goes away but the plan stays.

supporters_case.text: Common Cause New York recommends yes: "Reducing unnecessary administrative burdens can help smaller businesses and nonprofits participate in City contracting," and regular board meetings add oversight. Citizens Union also recommends yes, saying the changes "could improve it at the margins" by getting money out the door faster.

opponents_case.text: No group urging a no vote was found as of Oct 16. Citizens Union, which supports it, warns that letting the administration rewrite the vendor questionnaire carries risk because "some questions help ensure vendor integrity, prevent corruption, or hold vendors accountable," and wants the Department of Investigation involved. Vital City, also a supporter, says it lacks enforceable deadlines for registering contracts and paying vendors on time.

jurisdiction: City of New York (all five boroughs)
official_title: Proposal Number 3, a Question. Proposed Charter Amendment: Speed Up Street Safety Projects, Disposition of Unused City Property, Office Leasing. Simplify review of street safety projects to reduce construction timelines. Fast track disposition of unused City property with approval from City Planning Commission. Expedite leasing offices used for City workforce. "Yes" simplifies street project approval, City property disposition and office leasing. "No" maintains intra-agency consultation for road projects, Council approval for City property dispositions and Council disapproval of office leases.
plain_summary: Three changes in one vote. Street safety projects like bike and bus lanes need fewer internal check-ins. Small City-owned lots and air rights over City-owned landmarks can be sold or leased through a shorter review with no City Council vote. City office leases skip Planning Commission and Council review.
yes_means: Street safety projects face fewer required check-ins, small City lots and landmark air rights can be sold with no City Council vote, and City office leases skip Planning Commission and Council review.
no_means: Street projects keep their current check-ins, selling City property keeps its longer review with a City Council vote, and City office leases keep Planning Commission and Council review.
current_law: A "major transportation project" (a roadway change over four blocks or 1,000 feet, or any bike lane) requires notice to officials and the community board, consultation with the Police and Fire Departments, Small Business Services and the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, and the Fire Department must confer with nearby firehouses; DOT must certify all of it. Most sales and leases of City property go through ULURP, a roughly seven-month review ending with City Planning Commission and City Council votes. The no-auction sale of unbuildable lots expires in 2030. City office leases need a Planning Commission hearing and vote, and the Council can disapprove by a two-thirds vote.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal note was found. The Commission projects more than $200 million in City revenue from selling small surplus lots and landmark development rights, and says street projects would move at least 33% faster (13 of 37 major projects designated in 2025 were delayed past the 2026 construction season) and office leases up to 50 days faster.
pass_threshold: Simple majority of NYC voters who vote on the question. Each proposal passes or fails on its own.
confusing_wording_note: This bundles three unrelated changes, so you can't approve one part and reject another. 'Disposition' means selling or leasing City property. 'Unused City property' means City-owned lots under 10,000 square feet plus air rights over City-owned landmarks. 'Approval from City Planning Commission' means the Planning Commission, not the City Council, would have the final say. 'Intra-agency consultation' means agencies like the Fire Department checking with their own local units, such as nearby firehouses.

supporters_case.text: Citizens Union recommends yes, calling these "reasonable fixes": requiring approval from the Fire Department commissioner "instead of every affected firehouse" removes a mandate "that has caused delays and invited litigation," and it notes that "recent corruption scandals involving office leases were not uncovered through oversight by the City Council or City Planning Commission." Vital City, which also supports it, says the street piece "seems likely to expedite roadway improvements and save lives."

opponents_case.text: The Municipal Art Society recommends no, saying it "could make it easier to sell or transfer valuable public land and development rights without sufficient safeguards to ensure lasting public benefits." MAS says lots up to 10,000 square feet could serve affordable housing, parks, community gardens or flood protection, and wants public-benefit rules set before any fast-track sales. Common Cause New York takes no position on this one.

short_title: Street projects and city property review

jurisdiction: City of New York (all five boroughs)
official_title: Proposal Number 4, a Question. Proposed Charter Amendment: Simplify Building Permitting and Move Waterfront Permitting to Department of Buildings. Create centralized construction permits hub to simplify permitting. Move waterfront permitting from Department of Small Business Services to Department of Buildings. Allow construction approval by additional Department of Buildings officials. “Yes” simplifies permitting by authorizing a centralized permitting hub, moving waterfront permitting to Department of Buildings, and allowing additional Department of Buildings officials to issue approvals. “No” leaves laws unchanged.
plain_summary: Requires the Buildings Department to build one online hub for all City construction permits, by 2030 or later and if funded; each agency still does its own review. It also lets more Buildings officials approve plans and moves permits for piers and other waterfront structures to the Buildings Department.
yes_means: The Buildings Department must create one online hub for City construction permits, more Buildings officials can approve plans, and waterfront construction permits move to Buildings.
no_means: Builders keep applying through separate agency systems, approval power stays with a few Buildings officials, and Small Business Services keeps waterfront construction permits.
current_law: The Charter lets the Buildings commissioner appoint only two deputy commissioners and one borough superintendent per borough, and only they (or the commissioner) can approve construction documents. Each permitting agency runs its own submission system. Small Business Services handles permits for maritime structures and buildings on City-owned waterfront land.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal note was found. The permitting hub is "subject to budget appropriations." The Commission says the hub would bring 40 permits and approvals from 18 offices and agencies into one place.
pass_threshold: Simple majority of NYC voters who vote on the question. Each proposal passes or fails on its own.
confusing_wording_note: A 'permits hub' is one online front door, not a new agency; each agency keeps its own review and timeline, and the hub may not run until 2030 or later. 'Waterfront permitting' means construction-safety permits for piers and similar structures; it doesn't change what waterfront land can be used for.

supporters_case.text: Citizens Union, Common Cause New York and the Municipal Art Society all support it. Citizens Union calls the changes "positive modernization efforts that would make it easier to navigate the construction permitting process." Open New York, a pro-housing group, praised bringing approvals from 18 offices into one place.

opponents_case.text: No group urging a no vote was found as of Oct 16. Vital City, which supports it, says the hub is "helpful but not especially bold" because every agency keeps "the power to review and approve on its own schedule."

jurisdiction: City of New York (all five boroughs)
official_title: Proposal Number 5, a Question. Proposed Charter Amendment: Set Contribution Targets for Rainy Day Fund to Promote Sufficient Budgetary Reserves. Set target amount of money to hold in reserve funds, including rainy day fund, to address unexpected financial hardships in future years, and require development of methodology to calculate contributions. “Yes” requires Mayor to develop methodology for calculating deposits to rainy day fund, with deposits subject to approval in the City budget. “No” leaves laws unchanged, with no reserves target.
plain_summary: Sets a goal for City reserves equal to 12% of last year's tax revenue (the rainy day fund holds about $2 billion now). The mayor's budget office must publish a formula for deposits by May 2027. Actual deposits still need approval in each year's budget and can be skipped in hard times.
yes_means: The City sets a reserve goal of 12% of last year's tax revenue and must publish a formula for deposits, but each year's deposit still depends on the budget.
no_means: The rainy day fund stays as it is, with no reserve goal, no published deposit formula, and deposits decided in each year's budget.
current_law: The 2019 Charter amendment and a 2020 state law let the City keep a Revenue Stabilization Fund but require no deposits or minimum balance. Deposits are negotiated in each budget. State law already bars withdrawing more than 50% of the fund in a year unless the mayor certifies a compelling fiscal need. The fund held $1.969 billion when the Commission reported.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal note was found. The measure itself requires no spending; deposits remain subject to each year's budget. A 12% target would be roughly $11.5 billion by one estimate (Carol Kellermann, Vital City), versus about $2 billion in the fund today. The City Comptroller has recommended a 16% target.
pass_threshold: Simple majority of NYC voters who vote on the question. Each proposal passes or fails on its own.
confusing_wording_note: 'Set contribution targets' sounds like the City must save a set amount every year. It doesn't: deposits stay up to the mayor and Council in each budget and can be skipped in hard times, and the 12% goal can count other reserve funds too. A No vote doesn't abolish the rainy day fund, which already exists. People who want a stronger fund are split: some plan to vote No because 12% is too low, while others recommend Yes as a first step.

supporters_case.text: Citizens Union and Common Cause New York recommend yes. Common Cause says clearer rules "can make fiscal decisions more predictable and subject to public scrutiny" and give the elected Comptroller a formal role. Citizens Union calls it "an incremental step" that is "not perfect" but "a good proposal to strengthen the city's finances in the long run." The amNewYork editorial board urged voters in June to support a stronger rainy day fund (written before the final 12% text).

opponents_case.text: Citizens Budget Commission president Andrew Rein told The City he will vote no because the 12% benchmark is too low (the Comptroller recommends 16%), and said "as written, City policy could allow withdrawals for practically any reason and avoid deposits even when revenues are strong." Former CBC head Carol Kellermann, writing in Vital City, says it "creates a misleading impression" while leaving deposits in the mayor's hands. From the other side, some economists and City Council staff told the Commission that strict deposit and withdrawal rules could tie the City's hands in a crisis.
